claims.claim_vi: A stop-loss order sets a stop-loss price at which the investor will sell to limit loss; when the price hits that point the order is triggered and becomes a market order to sell at the current market price.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Example: an investor with 100 shares of a company at $40 wants to sell if the price falls to or below $36.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Execution: the investor submits the order; the trading engine creates it, subscribes to market data from the exchange, and when the price falls to, say, $35 submits a market order to sell 100 shares at the best price.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: The order is filled, usually instantly; the engine receives a fill report (here $35.5 per share) and notifies the investor.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Selling 100 shares at $35.5 yields $3,550 instead of the $3,600 that $36 would give; the difference ($50) is the lesson's arithmetic on the source's numbers.
claims.verified_by: Computed from the source example; no other source.

design_notes_vi: Một lược đồ ba bên với sáu thông điệp đúng thứ tự trong nguồn, và một khung ghi điều cần nhớ: giá kích hoạt chỉ đánh thức lệnh.
source_deviations: The source gives a list of steps; the lesson draws them as a sequence among three parties.
The lesson stresses that the stop price is a trigger and not a guaranteed sale price, which the source shows only through its numbers ($36 trigger, $35.5 fill).
The lesson mentions, as general knowledge, that other order types exist to limit the price paid; it does not describe them.
